q: Does cardiomyocyte loss leave uniformly smaller surviving cells?
o: All surviving cells become uniformly smaller
Those remaining cardiac myocytes are increased in size and are much more variable in size.
The largest surviving cells are the least vulnerable to stress
Surviving cells enlarge but become uniform in size
explanation:
Those remaining cardiac myocytes are increased in size and are much more variable in size. (p1116).

A. All surviving cells become uniformly smaller: The book describes increased and more variable size (p1116).
D. Surviving cells enlarge but become uniform in size: Size variability increases rather than disappears (p1116).
C. The largest surviving cells are the least vulnerable to stress: The largest cells are described as most vulnerable (p1116).

o: It must always be attributed solely to biological aging
mild disproportionate thickening of the basal ventricular septum
It reliably excludes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
It is defined by thinning of the basal ventricular septum
explanation:

C. It reliably excludes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: The morphology can confound that diagnosis rather than exclude it (p1119).
A. It must always be attributed solely to biological aging: The thickening may reflect hypertension rather than biological aging (p1119).

q: Does aortic sclerosis mean significant valvular obstruction?
o: A finding with no association with cardiovascular mortality
valve thickening without significant hemodynamic dysfunction
An inevitable progression to clinical aortic stenosis in every patient
Valve thickening that necessarily causes significant obstruction
explanation:
valve thickening without significant hemodynamic dysfunction (p1119).

D. Valve thickening that necessarily causes significant obstruction: The definition explicitly lacks significant hemodynamic dysfunction (p1119).
C. An inevitable progression to clinical aortic stenosis in every patient: The relationship to clinical stenosis is incompletely defined (p1119).
A. A finding with no association with cardiovascular mortality: Aortic sclerosis is associated with increased cardiovascular mortality (p1119).

q: Describe regurgitation compatible with normal aging.
o: always trivial or mild, central, and associated with normal (for age)-appearing leaflets
Severe regurgitation with normal aging as its sufficient explanation
Any leaflet appearance provided the patient is old
Any severity provided it is central
explanation:
always trivial or mild, central, and associated with normal (for age)-appearing leaflets (p1120).

B. Severe regurgitation with normal aging as its sufficient explanation: The described normal-aging pattern is always trivial or mild (p1120).
D. Any severity provided it is central: Central location alone is insufficient; the degree must be trivial or mild (p1120).
C. Any leaflet appearance provided the patient is old: The pattern includes normal-for-age leaflets, not arbitrary leaflet pathology (p1120).

q: Is a thin, hypermobile atrial septum the expected aging pattern?
o: Mobility with phasic respiration increases with age
The atrial septum thickens and becomes stiffer with age
A thin, hypermobile septum needs no further evaluation in an older person
A thin, hypermobile septum is the expected aging change
explanation:
The atrial septum thickens and becomes stiffer with age (p1120).

D. A thin, hypermobile septum is the expected aging change: That finding prompts investigation for aneurysm, PFO, or ASD (p1120).
A. Mobility with phasic respiration increases with age: The book describes reduced mobility (p1120).
C. A thin, hypermobile septum needs no further evaluation in an older person: Color Doppler and agitated-saline contrast evaluation are recommended for this unexpected finding (p1120).

q: Why does faster pulse-wave travel increase cardiac workload?
o: The reflected wave returns only after aortic valve closure and lowers systolic load
The reflected wave delays its return as arteries stiffen
Earlier reflected-wave arrival improves coronary perfusion without affecting LV afterload
arrive back at the heart before aortic valve closure, resulting in increased LV afterload
explanation:
arrive back at the heart before aortic valve closure, resulting in increased LV afterload (p1130-1131).

A. The reflected wave returns only after aortic valve closure and lowers systolic load: Return after closure describes the younger-heart timing; aging brings earlier return (p1130-1131).
B. The reflected wave delays its return as arteries stiffen: Stiffening increases pulse-wave velocity and brings earlier return (p1130-1131).
C. Earlier reflected-wave arrival improves coronary perfusion without affecting LV afterload: That benefit is associated with later, diastolic arrival; earlier arrival increases afterload (p1131).
